query.original_query: multilingual language model self-translation consistency answer reproducibility across paraphrases same language

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal mechanisms of self-translation consistency in multilingual language models, answer reproducibility across paraphrases, representation invariance in the residual stream and attention heads
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the internal mechanisms underlying self-translation consistency in multilingual language models, focusing on answer reproducibility across semantically equivalent paraphrases. Our analysis examines representation invariance within the residual stream and attention heads during multilingual factual recall. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize knowledge to specific MLP layers and attention heads, finding that consistent paraphrases activate overlapping feature subspaces in the residual stream, while inconsistent responses correspond to divergent attention patterns across languages. We further analyze the role of polysemantic neurons in the feed-forward layers, observing that feature superposition in higher layers correlates with reduced answer stability across paraphrases. Results show that attention heads in middle layers exhibit greater invariance to lexical variation, whereas later layers show sensitivity to surface-form changes. Our findings suggest that self-translation consistency is mediated by distributed, language-agnostic representations in early-to-middle layers, with later layers introducing language-specific biases that disrupt paraphrase invariance.

sub_queries.semantic_query: multilingual language processing and translation consistency in bilingual speakers, paraphrase and semantic invariance in human language comprehension, cross-linguistic representation
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the neural correlates of cross-linguistic semantic invariance during bilingual language comprehension. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we measured BOLD responses in balanced Spanish-English bilinguals as they performed a paraphrase judgment task. Participants read sentences in both languages and judged whether a subsequent sentence was a paraphrase of the original, regardless of language switch. We employed representational similarity analysis (RSA) to compare neural pattern similarity between within-language and cross-language paraphrase pairs. Results indicate that the left anterior temporal lobe and the angular gyrus exhibited higher representational similarity for semantically equivalent sentences across languages compared to unrelated sentences. Findings support the hypothesis that a shared, language-independent semantic representation is maintained in these regions. Furthermore, behavioral translation consistency, measured via a separate translation production task, correlated with the degree of cross-linguistic neural pattern similarity. These results suggest that the human language system relies on abstract semantic representations that are invariant across surface linguistic form, consistent with models of bilingual lexical-semantic organization.

papers.title: Do Multilingual Neural Machine Translation Models Contain Language Pair Specific Attention Heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual neural machine translation models contain language pair specific attention heads? The paper investigates this by analyzing individual attention heads in a many-to-one NMT model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in a multilingual NMT model, the most important attention heads are largely language-independent, and about 30% of heads can be pruned without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Although rare language-pair specific attention heads exist, the most important heads are language-independent, and around 30% of heads can be pruned without retraining and with almost no loss in BLEU.
papers.key_findings:
The set of most important attention heads is very similar across different language pairs.
It is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important attention heads without greatly hurting translation quality.
For encoder-decoder (cross) attention heads, the coverage metric is a better indicator for pruning importance, while for encoder self-attention heads, the confidence metric is more effective.
Some rare attention heads are language-pair specific, as identified by the exhaustive Sequential Backward Selection (SBS) procedure.
The variance, confidence, and coverage metrics provide a proxy for head importance, but the SBS algorithm yields the best ranking for pruning.
future_direction: Perform pruning at different levels of granularity (beyond single scalar metrics) to identify which parts of the model are more language-specific.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on the analysis of the multilingual representations focus on identifying whether there is an emergence of languageindependent representations, or whether a multilingual model partitions its weights among different languages. While most of such work has been conducted in a "black-box" manner, this paper aims to analyze individual components of a multilingual neural translation (NMT) model. In particular, we look at the encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention heads (in a many-to-one NMT model) that are more specific to the translation of a certain language pair than others by (1) employing metrics that quantify some aspects of the attention weights such as "variance" or "confidence", and (2) systematically ranking the importance of attention heads with respect to translation quality. Experimental results show that surprisingly, the set of most important attention heads are very similar across the language pairs and that it is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important heads without hurting the translation quality greatly.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: Are Knowledge and Reference in Multilingual Language Models Cross-Lingually Consistent?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models recall factual knowledge for coreferential statements in a similar manner across languages, how does the mechanism work, and which factors prevent model consistency in multilingual settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual consistency of factual knowledge in multilingual models, identifying bottlenecks related to language characteristics and showing that explicit cross-lingual supervision (code-switching, word alignment) improves consistency more than scaling or instruction tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights limitations in cross-lingual consistency of multilingual models and emphasizes the value of explicit cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for enhancing consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-lingual consistency is lower for languages dissimilar to English in script, family, or geography.
A consistency bottleneck exists in specific middle layers of the models.
Vocabulary expansion offers only slight consistency improvements and relies on deep semantic alignment rather than shared scripts.
Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives significantly improve consistency, while instruction tuning offers limited gains.
Activation patching on feed-forward neurons based on IG2 scores can partially calibrate consistency at test time, showing a causal relationship.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual consistency should be considered to assess cross-lingual transferability, maintain the factuality of the model knowledge across languages, and preserve the parity of language model performance. We are thus interested in analyzing, evaluating, and interpreting cross-lingual consistency for factual knowledge. To facilitate our study, we examine multiple pretrained models and tuned models with code-mixed coreferential statements that convey identical knowledge across languages. Interpretability approaches are leveraged to analyze the behavior of a model in cross-lingual contexts, showing different levels of consistency in multilingual models, subject to language families, linguistic factors, scripts, and a bottleneck in cross-lingual consistency on a particular layer. Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives show the most promising results, emphasizing the worthiness of cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for both multilingual performance and cross-lingual consistency enhancement. In addition, experimental results suggest promising result for calibrating consistency in the test time via activation patching.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in multilingual LLMs share similarities with English LLMs but with key differences, such as the role of MLPs in extraction and the composition of relation and language in the last token's function vector.
papers.conclusion: These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies—such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition—that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture.
Subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted.
In decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose relation and language in two separate stages.
MLPs play a more prominent role in extraction in multilingual LLMs compared to English LLMs.
papers.limitation: Excluded languages with too few examples, limiting the analysis to a subset of languages.
future_direction: Developing new methodologies for knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying whether models 'think' in English by examining how the function vector is altered across languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: An Underlying Mechanism for Language Latent Space Transitions in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: How do multilingual LLMs transfer representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space, and what neurons are responsible for this transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes and empirically validates the Transfer Neurons Hypothesis, identifying specific MLP neurons that facilitate transitions between language-specific and shared semantic latent spaces in multilingual LLMs, and shows their critical role in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that transfer neurons are a key mechanism for latent space transitions in multilingual LLMs, enabling language-agnostic reasoning and output generation in the input language.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations in multilingual LLMs form language-specific latent spaces in initial and final layers, converging to a shared semantic latent space in middle layers.
Transfer neurons in the MLP module are responsible for moving representations between language-specific and shared latent spaces.
Type-1 transfer neurons shift inputs to the shared space, while Type-2 neurons shift outputs back to language-specific spaces.
Type-2 neurons exhibit language specificity and are similar to previously identified language-specific neurons.
Deactivating transfer neurons impairs representation alignment and reduces performance on multilingual QA tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have suggested a processing framework for multilingual inputs in decoder-based LLMs: early layers convert inputs into English-centric and language-agnostic representations; middle layers perform reasoning within an English-centric latent space; and final layers generate outputs by transforming these representations back into language-specific latent spaces. However, the internal dynamics of such transformation and the underlying mechanism remain underexplored. Towards a deeper understanding of this framework, we propose and empirically validate The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: certain neurons in the MLP module are responsible for transferring representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space. Furthermore, we show that one function of language-specific neurons, as identified in recent studies, is to facilitate movement between latent spaces. Finally, we show that transfer neurons are critical for reasoning in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Paths Not Taken: Understanding and Mending the Multilingual Factual Recall Pipeline
papers.research_question: Why do multilingual large language models exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, and how can these failures be understood and mended?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a multilingual factual recall pipeline where LLMs use an English-centric mechanism and then translate answers, and introduces two vector interventions to fix errors in translation and recall, significantly improving cross-lingual factual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic insights into the multilingual processing pipeline can be used to design targeted, training-free interventions that direct the model toward better internal paths, unlocking latent multilingual capabilities and improving factual consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs employ a pipeline where factual information is first retrieved in English using intermediate English-centric mechanisms, followed by translation into the target language in later layers.
Two primary failure points cause cross-lingual inconsistencies: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric recall mechanism, and incorrect translation from English back to the target language.
A translation difference vector intervention, derived from the activation difference between explicit translation and fact-recall tasks, steers the model to use more effective translation components, improving conversion correctness.
A recall task vector intervention, extracted from in-context learning examples, promotes the engagement of English-centric factual recall components (like relation propagation and answer extraction) for multilingual prompts.
Combining both interventions leads to substantial improvements in factual recall accuracy, boosting performance by up to 37.6 percentage points for the lowest-performing language and an average gain of 19.04 points across all evaluated languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five non-English languages and ten relations on a single model (Llama-3.2-3B).
future_direction: Expanding the investigation to more diverse language families and syntactic structures.
Quantifying how the findings apply to relations of varying complexity or different models.
Developing automated methods to identify such weaknesses and implement corresponding solutions.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) often exhibit factual inconsistencies across languages, with significantly better performance in factual recall tasks in English than in other languages. The causes of these failures, however, remain poorly understood. Using mechanistic analysis techniques, we uncover the underlying pipeline that LLMs employ, which involves using the English-centric factual recall mechanism to process multilingual queries and then translating English answers back into the target language. We identify two primary sources of error: insufficient engagement of the reliable English-centric mechanism for factual recall, and incorrect translation from English back into the target language for the final answer. To address these vulnerabilities, we introduce two vector interventions, both independent of languages and datasets, to redirect the model toward better internal paths for higher factual consistency. Our interventions combined increase the recall accuracy by over 35 percent for the lowest-performing language. Our findings demonstrate how mechanistic insights can be used to unlock latent multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: On Neurons Invariant to Sentence Structural Changes in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How is sentence structure reflected in neural representations of machine translation systems, specifically examining neuron-level invariance to structural changes like active/passive voice and adverbial clause/noun phrase transformations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a model-agnostic methodology to analyze neuron activations across minimal paraphrases, finding that activation similarity is largely due to shallow features like word choice and sentence length, and demonstrates that sentence structure can be controlled via neuron manipulation, indicating distributed encoding.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that sentence structure distinctions are encoded in neural machine translation models and can be controlled via neuron manipulation, but the encoding is distributed and not localized to specific neurons. Future work should test additional architectures and language pairs.
papers.key_findings:
Similarity in neuron activations across paraphrases is mostly explained by shallow input features (word identity and positional encoding), not high-level abstractions.
Manipulating neuron activations can control the syntactic form of the output translation, showing that sentence structure distinctions are encoded in the model, albeit in a distributed manner.
The neurons most effective for manipulation are those most correlated across paraphrases (top ParaCorr), not those that vary the most, suggesting role polysemy and general importance.
The curated dataset of minimal paraphrase pairs and the semi-automatic generation method are provided for future research.
Correlation analysis must account for confounds like positional encoding and token overlap to avoid misleading conclusions.
papers.limitation:
Paraphrases may have unintended differences beyond the targeted structural change, introducing noise to the analysis.
The methodology is demonstrated on a specific Transformer model for English-German translation; insights may not generalize to other architectures or language pairs.
Aggregating token representations to sentence-level may lose encoded information.
Manipulation requires modifying a large number of neurons (at least 50%) and the effect is not always monotonic.
future_direction: Test additional architectures and language pairs.
Examine the representation significance of paraphrase pairs in other NLP tasks.
Explore non-linear manipulation techniques.
papers.abstract: We present a methodology that explores how sentence structure is reflected in neural representations of machine translation systems. We demonstrate our model-agnostic approach with the Transformer English-German translation model. We analyze neuron-level correlation of activations between paraphrases while discussing the methodology challenges and the need for confound analysis to isolate the effects of shallow cues. We find that similarity between activation patterns can be mostly accounted for by similarity in word choice and sentence length. Following that, we manipulate neuron activations to control the syntactic form of the output. We show this intervention to be somewhat successful, indicating that deep models capture sentence-structure distinctions, despite finding no such indication at the neuron level. To conduct our experiments, we develop a semi-automatic method to generate meaning-preserving minimal pair paraphrases (active-passive voice and adverbial clause-noun phrase) and compile a corpus of such pairs.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared cross-lingual abstractions, demonstrated via neuron analysis and manipulation.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, leading to the development of shared concept neurons across languages that encode generalized semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models initially form language-specific representations which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.
Language identification probing reveals a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons emerge as reliable predictors for the same semantic concepts across different languages, showing increasing alignment during training.
Neuron manipulation experiments demonstrate that concept-specific neurons identified from one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language once cross-lingual generalization is achieved.
The model's internal representations encode shared conceptual knowledge independent of the original language encoding.
papers.limitation: The number of publicly available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited, restricting the granularity of analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision.We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions.For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts.By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages.Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.This alignment manifests concretely in generation: once an MLLM exhibits cross-lingual generalization according to our measures, we can select concept-specific neurons identified from, e.g., Spanish text and manipulate them to guide token predictions.Remarkably, rather than generating Spanish text, the model produces semantically coherent English text.This demonstrates that cross-lingually aligned neurons encode generalized semantic representations, independent of the original language encoding.

papers.title: The Case for Translation-Invariant Self-Attention in Transformer-Based\n Language Models
papers.research_question: How are positional information encoded in transformer-based language models, and can translation-invariant self-attention be an effective alternative to conventional position embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), a new positional encoding method that satisfies six design criteria and improves performance on GLUE tasks with very few added parameters.
papers.conclusion: Translation invariance emerges in state-of-the-art language models, and TISA is a positional encoding method that satisfies all six design criteria and improves downstream performance.
papers.key_findings:
Position embeddings in transformer-based language models become increasingly translation-invariant during training, and this invariance correlates with model performance.
Adding TISA to ALBERT improves performance on GLUE tasks with minimal parameter increase.
TISA can be used with or without conventional position embeddings, though performance is better when combined.
papers.limitation:
Lack of computational resources to pretrain TISA-only models from scratch
TISA alone (without position embeddings) does not perform as well as when combined with position embeddings
future_direction: Applying TISA to transformer models in other domains like speech, motion synthesis, and computer vision
Exploring two-stage training with TISA, pre-training on short sequences and then scaling to longer ones
papers.abstract:
Mechanisms for encoding positional information are central for
transformer-based language models. In this paper, we analyze the position
embeddings of existing language models, finding strong evidence of translation
invariance, both for the embeddings themselves and for their effect on
self-attention. The degree of translation invariance increases during training
and correlates positively with model performance. Our findings lead us to
propose translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), which accounts for the
relative position between tokens in an interpretable fashion without needing
conventional position embeddings. Our proposal has several theoretical
advantages over existing position-representation approaches. Experiments show
that it improves on regular ALBERT on GLUE tasks, while only adding orders of
magnitude less positional parameters.

papers.title: Neuron Specialization: Leveraging intrinsic task modularity for multilingual machine translation
papers.research_question: How do neurons in multilingual translation models exhibit language-specific modularity, and can this be leveraged to reduce interference and improve translation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that FFN neurons in multilingual models exhibit language-specific modularity, and introduces Neuron Specialization, a method that leverages this to reduce interference and improve translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that intrinsic modularity in multilingual models can be leveraged to improve translation performance by reducing interference and enhancing transfer, with Neuron Specialization providing consistent gains.
papers.key_findings:
FFN neurons in multilingual translation models activate in a language-specific way, with overlaps indicating linguistic proximity.
The specialization of neurons evolves across layers, becoming more language-agnostic in the encoder and more specific in the decoder.
The proposed Neuron Specialization method, which updates task-specific neurons via sparse networks, consistently improves translation quality over baselines.
This method effectively reduces negative interference in high-resource languages and boosts knowledge transfer in low-resource languages.
Neuron Specialization is efficient, requiring minimal extra parameters and time compared to adapter-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to multilingual machine translation and does not explore other multilingual NLP tasks.
Analysis is confined to feed-forward network components, excluding other Transformer elements like attention mechanisms.
Neuron identification relies on ReLU activation states; other activation functions like GELU are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the exploration to a broader range of Multilingual Natural Language Processing tasks beyond translation.
Investigate the modularity of other Transformer components such as attention mechanisms or layer normalization.
Explore neuron specialization for FFNs using activation functions other than ReLU, such as GELU.
papers.abstract: Training a unified multilingual model promotes knowledge transfer but inevitably introduces negative interference. Language-specific modeling methods show promise in reducing interference. However, they often rely on heuristics to distribute capacity and struggle to foster cross-lingual transfer via isolated modules. In this paper, we explore intrinsic task modularity within multilingual networks and leverage these observations to circumvent interference under multilingual translation. We show that neurons in the feed-forward layers tend to be activated in a language-specific manner. Meanwhile, these specialized neurons exhibit structural overlaps that reflect language proximity, which progress across layers. Based on these findings, we propose Neuron Specialization, an approach that identifies specialized neurons to modularize feed-forward layers and then continuously updates them through sparse networks. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves consistent performance gains over strong baselines with additional analyses demonstrating reduced interference and increased knowledge transfer.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: How does Alignment Enhance LLMs' Multilingual Capabilities? A Language Neurons Perspective
papers.research_question: How does multilingual alignment enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities from the perspective of language neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a ternary classification of language neurons (specific, related, general) with an identification algorithm, and uses it to analyze how multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' capabilities by promoting shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a ternary neuron classification and shows that multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' multilingual capabilities by promoting shared language-related neurons, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Language-related neurons shared by multiple languages are crucial for multilingual performance, not just language-specific neurons.
Multilingual alignment increases the reliance on shared language-related neurons rather than language-specific neurons.
LLMs' internal multilingual inference process can be divided into four functional stages based on neuron distributions.
Alignment enhances the activation of appropriate neuron types across different stages of inference.
Spontaneous multilingual alignment is facilitated by increased sharing of language-related neurons across languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited experiments on only two models and two datasets due to resource constraints.
No finer-grained analysis of neurons within the same layer.
future_direction: Perform more comprehensive analysis on different models and datasets.
Conduct finer-grained analysis of neurons within layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Alignment is an effective and representative paradigm to enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities, which transfers the capabilities from the high-resource languages to the low-resource languages. Meanwhile, some research on language-specific neurons provides a new perspective to analyze and understand LLMs' mechanisms. However, we find that there are many neurons that are shared by multiple but not all languages and cannot be correctly classified. In this work, we propose a ternary classification methodology that categorizes neurons into three types, including language-specific neurons, language-related neurons, and general neurons. And we propose a corresponding identification algorithm to distinguish these different types of neurons. Furthermore, based on the distributional characteristics of different types of neurons, we divide the LLMs' internal process for multilingual inference into four parts: (1) multilingual understanding, (2) shared semantic space reasoning, (3) multilingual output space transformation, and (4) vocabulary space outputting. Additionally, we systematically analyze the models before and after alignment with a focus on different types of neurons. We also analyze the phenomenon of ''Spontaneous Multilingual Alignment''. Overall, our work conducts a comprehensive investigation based on different types of neurons, providing empirical results and valuable insights to better understand multilingual alignment and multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Viewing Knowledge Transfer in Multilingual Machine Translation Through a Representational Lens
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between cross-lingual knowledge transfer and representational similarities in multilingual neural machine translation, and can we develop a better measure for transfer than translation quality alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), a measure of knowledge transfer based on representational similarities between languages in multilingual machine translation, and proposes a novel training scheme with an auxiliary similarity loss that improves translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) is a better measure of knowledge transfer than translation quality alone, and that explicitly optimizing for language invariance using multi-parallel data improves translation for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Representational Transfer Potential (RTP) can measure both positive and negative transfer and is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality (BLEU), indicating that improvements are due to knowledge transfer and not just increased target data.
Multi-parallel overlap between languages is a highly predictive yet under-explored feature for transfer.
A training method that uses an auxiliary similarity loss to encourage language-invariant representations yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.
RTP can be used to identify suitable auxiliary transfer languages, with training on top RTP contributors leading to substantially better results than training on bottom contributors.
Dataset features (multi-parallel overlap, source subword overlap, vocabulary occupancy) are more predictive of representational similarity than linguistic features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English-centric many-to-many and many-to-English models, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other multilingual settings.
The training data size (TED corpus) is relatively small compared to other datasets like OPUS-100, which may affect model performance.
papers.abstract: We argue that translation quality alone is not a sufficient metric for measuring knowledge transfer in multilingual neural machine translation. To support this claim, we introduce Representational Transfer Potential (RTP), which measures representational similarities between languages. We show that RTP can measure both positive and negative transfer (interference), and find that RTP is strongly correlated with changes in translation quality, indicating that transfer does occur. Furthermore, we investigate data and language characteristics that are relevant for transfer, and find that multi-parallel overlap is an important yet under-explored feature. Based on this, we develop a novel training scheme, which uses an auxiliary similarity loss that encourages representations to be more invariant across languages by taking advantage of multi-parallel data. We show that our method yields increased translation quality for low- and mid-resource languages across multiple data and model setups.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: On the Entity-Level Alignment in Crosslingual Consistency
papers.research_question: What factors give rise to crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and do failures in entity alignment cause inconsistencies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis linking crosslingual consistency to entity-level alignment, introduces two prompting methods (SUBSUB and SUBINJ) that improve factual recall and consistency, and uses mechanistic interpretability to show these methods enhance entity representation alignment through pivot-language processing.
papers.conclusion: Entity alignment is a key factor underlying crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and the proposed prompting methods offer effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction by enhancing this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Crosslingual consistency is strongly correlated with entity alignment across all studied models.
Consistent factual recall rarely occurs without correctly aligning either the subject or object entities between two languages.
The proposed prompting methods SUBSUB and SUBINJ, which incorporate English translations of subjects, substantially improve factual recall accuracy and consistency, especially in English-centric models.
Mechanistic analysis using Logit Lens shows that SUBSUB and SUBINJ interventions reinforce entity representation alignment in the model's internal conceptual space.
The model's conceptual space is biased towards high-resource languages like English, explaining why using English subject translations is more effective than using other languages.
papers.limitation: Inconsistency can also stem from failure in the processing stage – i.e., the model lacks the factual knowledge so it cannot retrieve the correct object in the conceptual space, which is beyond the scope of this paper.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are expected to recall factual knowledge consistently across languages. However, the factors that give rise to such crosslingual consistency -- and its frequent failure -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we hypothesize that these inconsistencies may arise from failures in entity alignment, the process of mapping subject and object entities into a shared conceptual space across languages. To test this, we assess alignment through entity-level (subject and object) translation tasks, and find that consistency is strongly correlated with alignment across all studied models, with misalignment of subjects or objects frequently resulting in inconsistencies. Building on this insight, we propose SubSub and SubInj, two effective methods that integrate English translations of subjects into prompts across languages, leading to substantial gains in both factual recall accuracy and consistency. Finally, our mechanistic analysis reveals that these interventions reinforce the entity representation alignment in the conceptual space through model's internal pivot-language processing, offering effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities.
