In this work, we trace LLMs' internal cultural understanding mechanisms by measuring activation path overlaps when answering semantically equivalent questions under two conditions: varying the target country while fixing the question language, and varying the question language while fixing the country. We also use same-language country pairs to disentangle language from cultural aspects. Results show that internal paths overlap more for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, indicating strong language-specific patterns. Notably, the South Korea-North Korea pair exhibits low overlap and high variability, showing that linguistic similarity does not guarantee aligned internal representation.

papers.title: Triangulation as an Acceptance Rule for Multilingual Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we validate mechanistic explanations for multilingual models to ensure they are causal and invariant across languages and scripts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces triangulation, an acceptance rule for mechanistic interpretability that requires necessity, sufficiency, and invariance across predicate-preserving environments to filter spurious circuits.
papers.conclusion: Triangulation offers a concrete step toward rigorous, transferable mechanistic explanations by requiring cross-environment consistency, allowing circuits that pass to be interpreted with greater confidence as capturing language-agnostic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.
Triangulation can be extended to multimodal settings by holding the image fixed and varying the prompt language.
Triangulation enables separation of circuits into visual, linguistic, and spurious categories based on cross-environment invariance.
The method is grounded in causal abstraction theory and provides an approximate transformation score over interchange interventions.
Triangulation requires explicit cue-only falsifiers to reject mechanisms that rely on surface cues rather than predicate information.
papers.limitation:
Multiple circuits may satisfy triangulation if their effects are redundant; triangulation identifies sufficient mechanisms but does not guarantee uniqueness.
The quality of reference families is decisive, and poor-quality families can mislead by either accepting spurious circuits or rejecting genuine circuits.
Causal interventions at scale are computationally expensive, and prioritization strategies are advisable for practical deployment.
When using LLM judges to verify predicate preservation, circularity risks arise if the judge correlates with the model under study.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models achieve strong aggregate performance yet often behave unpredictably across languages, scripts, and cultures. We argue that mechanistic explanations for such models should satisfy a \emph{causal} standard: claims must survive causal interventions and must \emph{cross-reference} across environments that perturb surface form while preserving meaning. We formalize \emph{reference families} as predicate-preserving variants and introduce \emph{triangulation}, an acceptance rule requiring necessity (ablating the circuit degrades the target behavior), sufficiency (patching activations transfers the behavior), and invariance (both effects remain directionally stable and of sufficient magnitude across the reference family). To supply candidate subgraphs, we adopt automatic circuit discovery and \emph{accept or reject} those candidates by triangulation. We ground triangulation in causal abstraction by casting it as an approximate transformation score over a distribution of interchange interventions, connect it to the pragmatic interpretability agenda, and present a comparative experimental protocol across multiple model families, language pairs, and tasks. Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Confusion in English-Centric Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does language confusion arise mechanistically in English-centric LLMs, and can it be mitigated through neuron-level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of language confusion in LLMs, revealing that confusion points arise from transition failures in final layers and can be effectively mitigated by editing a small set of critical neurons identified through comparative analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability account of language confusion in English-centric LLMs, demonstrating that targeted neuron editing can robustly mitigate confusion without sacrificing general competence or fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Confusion points are critical drivers of language confusion, and token replacement at these points reduces confusion.
Layer-wise analysis shows that language confusion is caused by failed transitions to the target language in the final layers.
Neuron-level analysis identifies specific FFN neurons in late layers that are responsible for confusion points.
Comparative importance selection of neurons enables effective mitigation of language confusion through editing.
Neuron editing achieves confusion reduction comparable to multilingual tuning for many languages while preserving general competence and output quality.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on the monolingual setting; cross-lingual contexts are left for future research.
Neuron editing interventions may require further validation across broader domains and model architectures.
Fully understanding how these mechanisms interact with other multilingual phenomena warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Extending analysis to cross-lingual contexts
Validating neuron editing across broader domains and model architectures
Investigating interactions with other multilingual phenomena
papers.abstract: Language confusion -- where large language models (LLMs) generate unintended languages against the user's need -- remains a critical challenge, especially for English-centric models. We present the first mechanistic interpretability (MI) study of language confusion, combining behavioral benchmarking with neuron-level analysis. Using the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB), we show that confusion points (CPs) -- specific positions where language switches occur -- are central to this phenomenon. Through layer-wise analysis with TunedLens and targeted neuron attribution, we reveal that transition failures in the final layers drive confusion. We further demonstrate that editing a small set of critical neurons, identified via comparative analysis with a multilingual-tuned counterpart, substantially mitigates confusion while largely preserving general competence and fluency. Our approach matches multilingual alignment in confusion reduction for many languages and yields cleaner, higher-quality outputs. These findings provide new insights into the internal dynamics of LLMs and highlight neuron-level interventions as a promising direction for robust, interpretable multilingual language modeling. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ercong21/lang_confusion.

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Handle Multilingualism?
papers.research_question: How do large language models handle multilingualism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and verifies a three-stage multilingual workflow (MWork) in LLMs, introducing PLND to detect language-specific neurons and showing how fine-tuning these neurons enhances multilingual abilities.
papers.conclusion: The verified MWork explains how LLMs handle multilingual tasks and provides an effective method for language-specific enhancement through fine-tuning language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs convert multilingual inputs to English in intermediate layers for task-solving and then revert to the original language for generation.
Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection (PLND) can identify language-specific neurons without any labeled data.
Deactivating language-specific neurons causes significant performance drops in multilingual tasks but minimal impact on English.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons with small datasets (e.g., 400 documents) improves multilingual performance without compromising other languages.
The multilingual workflow involves understanding layers, task-solving layers for reasoning and knowledge extraction, and generation layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning with too many documents can lead to overfitting and performance deterioration due to disruption of original knowledge distribution.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse languages. This study explores how LLMs handle multilingualism. Based on observed language ratio shifts among layers and the relationships between network structures and certain capabilities, we hypothesize the LLM's multilingual workflow ($\texttt{MWork}$): LLMs initially understand the query, converting multilingual inputs into English for task-solving. In the intermediate layers, they employ English for thinking and incorporate multilingual knowledge with self-attention and feed-forward structures, respectively. In the final layers, LLMs generate responses aligned with the original language of the query. To verify $\texttt{MWork}$, we introduce Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection ($\texttt{PLND}$) to identify activated neurons for inputs in different languages without any labeled data. Using $\texttt{PLND}$, we validate $\texttt{MWork}$ through extensive experiments involving the deactivation of language-specific neurons across various layers and structures. Moreover, $\texttt{MWork}$ allows fine-tuning of language-specific neurons with a small dataset, enhancing multilingual abilities in a specific language without compromising others. This approach results in an average improvement of $3.6\%$ for high-resource languages and $2.3\%$ for low-resource languages across all tasks with just $400$ documents.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does self-repair exist across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution, and what are the mechanisms behind it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that self-repair exists across model families and sizes on the full pretraining distribution, and identifies two contributing mechanisms: changes in the LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing anti-erasure.
papers.conclusion: Self-repair is a real phenomenon that complicates interpretability efforts, and the findings provide evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis as a framework that predicts self-repair.
papers.key_findings:
Self-repair exists across model families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution.
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, with the degree of compensation varying significantly across prompts.
A nontrivial fraction (around 30%) of self-repair can be attributed to changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor.
Sparse sets of neurons in MLP layers implement anti-erasure, contributing to self-repair, but the specific neurons vary across prompts.
Self-repair complicates interpretability efforts that rely on ablation-based metrics.
papers.limitation:
Self-repair is imperfect and noisy, making it difficult to quantify precisely.
Ablations take models off-distribution, leading to unpredictable and hard-to-interpret consequences.
future_direction: Control how far from distribution causal interventions take the model, e.g., by avoiding zero ablation or freezing LayerNorm.
Use path patching instead of patching full components to reduce off-distribution effects.
Further investigate the Iterative Inference hypothesis as an explanation for self-repair.
papers.abstract: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect). We highlight two different mechanisms that contribute to self-repair, including changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. We additionally discuss the implications of these results for interpretability practitioners and close with a more speculative discussion on the mystery of why self-repair occurs in these models at all, highlighting evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis in language models, a framework that predicts self-repair.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Unveiling Multilinguality in Transformer Models: Exploring Language Specificity in Feed-Forward Networks
papers.research_question: Do neurons in the feed-forward networks of multilingual transformer models exhibit language-specific or language-agnostic behavior across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in multilingual transformer models, feed-forward network layers near the input and output are more language-specific, whereas middle layers are more language-agnostic.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language specificity in FFNs is higher near the input and output layers, and training data imbalance influences detector activations.
papers.key_findings:
Layers closest to the input and output exhibit more language-specific behavior compared to middle layers.
The number of detectors triggered by English prefixes is higher than for Czech, reflecting training data imbalance.
The number of unique detectors varies across layers, with sparsity patterns observed in FFN activations.
Linear classifiers can predict the language of input prefixes from detector activations with higher accuracy in input and output layers.
Czech-specific detectors decrease in middle layers, suggesting semantic processing uses more language-agnostic detectors.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to only the XGLM model.
Study is centred on the Czech-English language pair, and findings may not generalize to other languages.
Lack of qualitative analysis of linguistic cues triggering detector activation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more language pairs and other multilingual autoregressive language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that the feed-forward module within Transformers can be viewed as a collection of key-value memories, where the keys learn to capture specific patterns from the input based on the training examples. The values then combine the output from the 'memories' of the keys to generate predictions about the next token. This leads to an incremental process of prediction that gradually converges towards the final token choice near the output layers. This interesting perspective raises questions about how multilingual models might leverage this mechanism. Specifically, for autoregressive models trained on two or more languages, do all neurons (across layers) respond equally to all languages? No! Our hypothesis centers around the notion that during pretraining, certain model parameters learn strong language-specific features, while others learn more language-agnostic (shared across languages) features. To validate this, we conduct experiments utilizing parallel corpora of two languages that the model was initially pretrained on. Our findings reveal that the layers closest to the network's input or output tend to exhibit more language-specific behaviour compared to the layers in the middle.

papers.title: Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions: Toward Interpretable and Efficient Multilingual Control for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode language identity, and can we identify sparse, consistent dimensions that control the cross-lingual transition from shared representations to language-specific token spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that cross-lingual transfer in LLMs is governed by a sparse, consistent set of language-specific dimensions in the residual stream, and introduces a training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions for controlled language switching.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific dimensions are a consistent and controllable mechanism underlying cross-lingual transfer in LLMs, enabling efficient and interpretable multilingual control through simple, training-free interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific dimensions are sparse and appear at consistent indices across intermediate to final layers of LLMs.
These dimensions can be identified with as few as 50 sentences of parallel or monolingual data.
Intervening on these dimensions by overwriting their values can switch the model's output language while preserving semantic content.
The proposed method outperforms prior neuron-based approaches (Neuron-Kojima and Neuron-Tang) on a multilingual generation control task.
There is significant overlap in language-specific dimensions across typologically similar languages (e.g., Chinese and Japanese share many dimensions).
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters (e.g., anchor layer, scaling coefficient) were primarily tuned on Llama2-7B and transferred to other models (Llama3.1-8B, Aya23-8B), which may be suboptimal.
Evaluation is limited to multilingual generation control and question answering tasks; broader impact on downstream tasks (e.g., mathematics, summarization) and robustness across prompt formulations remains unexamined.
future_direction: Conduct systematic per-model hyperparameter search to optimize performance for each model individually.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of downstream tasks, incorporate task-specific metrics and human judgments, and assess robustness across different prompt formulations.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities despite limited exposure to non-English data. Prior studies show that English-centric large language models map multilingual content into English-aligned representations at intermediate layers and then project them back into target-language token spaces in the final layer. From this observation, we hypothesize that this cross-lingual transition is governed by a small and sparse set of dimensions, which occur at consistent indices across the intermediate to final layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions, requiring only as few as 50 sentences of either parallel or monolingual data. Experiments on a multilingual generation control task reveal the interpretability of these dimensions, demonstrating that the interventions in these dimensions can switch the output language while preserving semantic content, and that it surpasses the performance of prior neuron-based approaches at a substantially lower cost.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models, and what are the properties of the neurons that store such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization in multilingual PLMs, and discovers two new types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons.
papers.conclusion: The AMIG method effectively localizes knowledge neurons in multilingual PLMs, and the discoveries of language-independent and degenerate knowledge neurons shed light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AMIG method localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than baseline methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons exist, are concentrated in the final layers, and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist, exhibit functional overlap, and can be used to help PLMs detect wrong facts in a fact-checking task.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models (BERT and GPT-2).
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration on knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Disentangling meaning from language in LLM-based machine translation
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally encode and distribute translation functions, specifically target language identification and sentence equivalence, at the sentence level?
papers.core_contribution: Translation in LLMs is implemented by sparse, distinct sets of attention heads for target language identification and sentence equivalence; steering these heads enables instruction-free machine translation performance comparable to instruction-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Translation in LLMs is implemented by sparse, specialized attention heads for language and equivalence, and these representations are transferable and can be steered to control translation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of attention heads (≈1%) play a considerable role in MT performance across all pairs, demonstrating that translation is mechanistically localized.
Target language identification and sentence equivalence are encoded by distinct, separable sets of heads.
This organization holds across 20 translation directions.
Steering vectors built from these heads enable instruction-free MT performance comparable to instruction-based prompting.
Ablating these heads selectively disrupts their corresponding translation functions.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to explain how neural networks implement their capabilities, but the scale of Large Language Models (LLMs) has limited prior MI work in Machine Translation (MT) to word-level analyses. We study sentence-level MT from a mechanistic perspective by analyzing attention heads to understand how LLMs internally encode and distribute translation functions. We decompose MT into two subtasks: producing text in the target language (i.e. target language identification) and preserving the input sentence's meaning (i.e. sentence equivalence). Across three families of open-source models and 20 translation directions, we find that distinct, sparse sets of attention heads specialize in each subtask. Based on this insight, we construct subtask-specific steering vectors and show that modifying just 1% of the relevant heads enables instruction-free MT performance comparable to instruction-based prompting, while ablating these heads selectively disrupts their corresponding translation functions.

papers.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
papers.research_question: How sensitive are neural language model representations to prior context, and how do these representations compare to human brain activations during story reading?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Stability Analysis (ReStA) to analyze context-dependence in neural language models, finding that LSTM-based models are more similar to brain representations than transformer-based models, and that deeper layers are more context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: ReStA and RSA are useful for comparing models and brains, but caution is required due to low correlations. LSTM-based models are more similar to brain data, and brain data may only reflect shallow linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based models (GoogleLM and ELMO) show higher similarity between their two layers compared to BERT.
For LSTM-based models, the first layer is less sensitive to context length than the last layer, suggesting a hierarchical encoding mechanism.
Transformer-based models (BERT) are more sensitive to context length overall, and their first layer is more context-dependent than the last layer.
Among the models, UniSentEnc learns very different representations from the others, possibly due to different training objectives.
LSTM-based models achieve higher similarity with brain data compared to GloVe and transformer-based models, and their lower layers align better with brain representations.
papers.limitation:
Standard RSA assumes all features of the representational spaces have equal contributions, leading to information loss.
The representational similarity between all models and the brain images remains very low.
Inherent issues in the brain data (e.g., hemodynamic response delay, noise) and complexity of the story reading task make evaluation hard.
future_direction: Perform further analysis on various (bigger) datasets to better interpret what is happening in both the brain and computational models.
Postpone further analysis with the predictive approach (linear regression) to future studies.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define and apply representational stability analysis (ReStA), an intuitive way of analyzing neural language models. ReStA is a variant of the popular representational similarity analysis (RSA) in cognitive neuroscience. While RSA can be used to compare representations in models, model components, and human brains, ReStA compares instances of the same model, while systematically varying single model parameter. Using ReStA, we study four recent and successful neural language models, and evaluate how sensitive their internal representations are to the amount of prior context. Using RSA, we perform a systematic study of how similar the representational spaces in the first and second (or higher) layers of these models are to each other and to patterns of activation in the human brain. Our results reveal surprisingly strong differences between language models, and give insights into where the deep linguistic processing, that integrates information over multiple sentences, is happening in these models. The combination of ReStA and RSA on models and brains allows us to start addressing the important question of what kind of linguistic processes we can hope to observe in fMRI brain imaging data. In particular, our results suggest that the data on story reading from Wehbe et al. (2014) contains a signal of shallow linguistic processing, but show no evidence on the more interesting deep linguistic processing.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons: The Key to Multilingual Capabilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models process multilingual texts, and can we identify language-specific neurons that are key to their multilingual capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language activation probability entropy (LAPE) to identify language-specific neurons in LLMs, and finds that a small subset of neurons in the top and bottom layers is crucial for multilingual processing, enabling steering of output language.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces LAPE to identify language-specific neurons, finds that a small subset of neurons in top/bottom layers are key to multilingual processing, and demonstrates that output language can be steered by manipulating these neurons.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of neurons (identified by LAPE) is crucial for processing a particular language; deactivating them severely degrades performance in that language.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in the top and bottom layers of the transformer, with bottom layers mapping to a shared semantic space and top layers mapping to language-specific vocabulary.
Larger models tend to have neurons specialized for single languages, while smaller models may share neurons across languages.
Chinese and Japanese share many language-specific neurons, likely due to character overlap.
Selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons can steer the output language of the model, mitigating off-target language issues.
papers.limitation:
The method is relative to the presence of multiple languages and cannot establish an absolute threshold for single-language scenarios.
The criteria for distinguishing high-resource and low-resource languages need further investigation.
The research only begins to explore steering output language; strategies to enhance multilingual proficiency are still needed.
future_direction: Enhance knowledge transfer between major and minor languages.
Devise efficient strategies for continual pre-training to better accommodate specific languages.
Investigate the model's ability to manage a large number of languages and the differences between languages.
papers.abstract: Tianyi Tang, Wenyang Luo, Haoyang Huang, Dongdong Zhang, Xiaolei Wang, Xin Zhao, Furu Wei, Ji-Rong Wen. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Mitigating Negative Interference in Multilingual Knowledge Editing through Null-Space Constraints
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently update knowledge in multilingual large language models sequentially across languages without causing negative interference and while preserving multilingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LangEdit, a null-space constrained framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that projects parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: LangEdit is an effective framework for multilingual sequential knowledge editing that uses null-space projection to isolate language-specific updates, mitigating negative interference and preserving multilingual generalization, as demonstrated across multiple models and languages.
papers.key_findings:
LangEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in multilingual sequential knowledge editing, improving editing accuracy and multilingual generalization across three model architectures and six languages.
LangEdit effectively mitigates negative interference by projecting language-specific updates onto the null space of previous updates, preserving performance in previously edited languages.
The method demonstrates cross-lingual knowledge transfer, where edits in one language can be accessed in another without explicit editing in that language.
Editing effectiveness varies by language, with languages having less pretraining data (e.g., Spanish) showing greater improvement than high-resource languages (e.g., English).
LangEdit maintains high specificity, ensuring that edits do not affect unrelated knowledge, and improves downstream task performance on multilingual benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on 6-8B parameter LLMs; extending to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) could reveal scaling effects.
The current evaluation focuses on constrained editing scenarios; future work should explore a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Multilingual experiments are limited to 6 languages; developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages would better test the boundaries of LangEdit and baselines.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger architectures (e.g., 70B-scale models) to reveal scaling effects.
Exploring a broader range of downstream applications to assess real-world deployment viability.
Developing comprehensive multilingual benchmarks covering hundreds of languages.
