Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is gender represented in multilingual models? Is the gender concept encoded in shared subspaces across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Gender representation in multilingual models consists of both shared and language-specific components. The most dominant gender directions are shared across languages, enabling good cross-lingual gender classification, but language-specific directions prevent effective cross-lingual gender removal.
papers.conclusion: Gender representation in multilingual models is partially shared across languages, with the most salient directions being shared and less salient ones being language-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Gender classification using linear probes transfers well across languages (English, French, Spanish).
Gender removal using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) does not transfer well across languages.
Gender subspaces are spanned by a few dominant directions that are shared across languages and other language-specific directions.
The shared gender directions are the most dominant ones (highest predictive power).
The partial sharing explains the discrepancy between transferable classification and non-transferable removal.
papers.limitation:
The study relies on a narrow, binary notion of gender, which does not reflect the full complexity of gender bias.
The analysis is limited to three languages (English, French, Spanish) due to dataset availability.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models were shown to allow for nontrivial transfer across scripts and languages. In this work, we study the structure of the internal representations that enable this transfer. We focus on the representation of gender distinctions as a practical case study, and examine the extent to which the gender concept is encoded in shared subspaces across different languages. Our analysis shows that gender representations consist of several prominent components that are shared across languages, alongside language-specific components. The existence of language-independent and language-specific components provides an explanation for an intriguing empirical observation we make: while gender classification transfers well across languages, interventions for gender removal, trained on a single language, do not transfer easily to others.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Do LLMs Need to Think in One Language? Correlation between Latent Language and Task Performance
papers.research_question: Does consistency in the latent language used by LLMs during internal reasoning enhance downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that LLMs do not always need to think consistently in one language for optimal task performance, as they can adapt internal representations in later layers to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The initial hypothesis that consistency in latent language enhances performance is contradicted; models do not always need to think in one language consistently for optimal performance.
papers.key_findings:
Disrupting latent language with adversarial prompts does not always degrade task performance.
Models can flexibly adjust their latent language depending on input language.
Higher proportions of adversarial prompts generally reduce robustness.
The correlation between latent language consistency and robustness varies across models and tasks.
Models adapt their internal representations near the final layers to match the target language, reducing the impact of consistency on overall performance.
papers.limitation:
The approach for determining dominant language (LLC Score) may not be the best.
Effects may depend on specific adversarial prompts used.
Analysis limited to relatively small models; extension to larger models is future work.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models with more extensive noise injection using multiple GPUs.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to process information using a proficient internal language consistently, referred to as latent language, which may differ from the input or output languages. However, how the discrepancy between the latent language and the input and output language affects downstream task performance remains largely unexplored. While many studies research the latent language of LLMs, few address its importance in influencing task performance. In our study, we hypothesize that thinking in latent language consistently enhances downstream task performance. To validate this, our work varies the input prompt languages across multiple downstream tasks and analyzes the correlation between consistency in latent language and task performance. We create datasets consisting of questions from diverse domains such as translation and geo-culture, which are influenced by the choice of latent language. Experimental results across multiple LLMs on translation and geo-culture tasks, which are sensitive to the choice of language, indicate that maintaining consistency in latent language is not always necessary for optimal downstream task performance. This is because these models adapt their internal representations near the final layers to match the target language, reducing the impact of consistency on overall performance.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: SteerEval: Inference-time Interventions Strengthen Multilingual Generalization in Neural Summarization Metrics
papers.research_question: Does steering activations toward an English pivot improve correlation with human judgments for multilingual neural metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering at inference time improves the correlation of multilingual neural metrics with human judgments for summarization evaluation across diverse languages.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering strengthens multilingual generalization in neural metrics, demonstrating the utility of model-internal insights for practical evaluation scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Steering activations toward English improves Pearson correlation with human judgments for both encoder-based and LLM-based metrics.
Vector-based steering tends to produce larger improvements than map-based steering, especially for low-performing language-metric pairs.
COMET, an encoder-based metric, shows significant gains from steering, indicating the method's applicability beyond LLMs.
Languages with initially low correlation, such as Hebrew and Yoruba, benefit the most from steering interventions.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the steering factor, with optimal values varying across languages and dimensions.
papers.limitation:
Smaller count of samples and human annotators in certain languages for the primary dataset.
Lack of a development set to tune the steering parameters ρ and σ.
Specific source-target language pairs might be more effective than using English as the sole pivot.
future_direction: Investigate combining language- and dimension-specific interventions for multilingual evaluation.
Explore alternative pivot languages beyond English and French.
papers.abstract: An increasing body of work has leveraged multilingual language models for Natural Language Generation tasks such as summarization. A major empirical bottleneck in this area is the shortage of accurate and robust evaluation metrics for many languages, which hinders progress. Recent studies suggest that multilingual language models often use English as an internal pivot language, and that misalignment with this pivot can lead to degraded downstream performance. Motivated by the hypothesis that this mismatch could also apply to multilingual neural metrics, we ask whether steering their activations toward an English pivot can improve correlation with human judgments. We experiment with encoder- and decoder-based metrics and find that test-time intervention methods are effective across the board, increasing metric effectiveness for diverse languages.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: First Align, then Predict: Understanding the Cross-Lingual Ability of Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What parts of the model and what mechanisms support zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual BERT?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT operates as the stacking of two modules: a multilingual encoder in the lower layers critical for cross-lingual transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little importance for transfer.
papers.conclusion: mBERT is constructed from a multilingual encoder in the lower layers that aligns representations across languages and is critical for cross-language transfer, and a task-specific, language-agnostic predictor in the upper layers that has little effect on transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of mBERT are critical for cross-lingual transfer, while upper layers are task-specific and language-agnostic.
Cross-lingual similarity (CKA) between representations of source and target languages is highest in the middle layers and strongly correlates with cross-lingual performance.
Randomly initializing lower layers harms cross-lingual performance but not same-language performance, indicating their specific role in cross-lingual alignment.
The cross-lingual alignment learned during pretraining is preserved after fine-tuning.
This mechanism suggests mBERT reproduces the standard cross-lingual pipeline without explicit supervision.
future_direction: Using the findings to design better multilingual pre-training processes.
Inspecting the mismatch with Singh et al. (2019) who found no language alignment across layers for Natural Language Inference.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot crosslingual transfer capabilities. Such transfer emerges by fine-tuning on a task of interest in one language and evaluating on a distinct language, not seen during the fine-tuning. Despite promising results, we still lack a proper understanding of the source of this transfer. Using a novel layer ablation technique and analyses of the model's internal representations, we show that multilingual BERT, a popular multilingual language model, can be viewed as the stacking of two sub-networks: a multilingual encoder followed by a taskspecific language-agnostic predictor. While the encoder is crucial for cross-lingual transfer and remains mostly unchanged during finetuning, the task predictor has little importance on the transfer and can be reinitialized during fine-tuning. We present extensive experiments with three distinct tasks, seventeen typologically diverse languages and multiple domains to support our hypothesis.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy\n Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads to translation performance? Do they play consistent and interpretable roles? Can the number of heads be significantly reduced without serious performance loss?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that only a subset of attention heads are important for translation, with interpretable functions, and introduces a pruning method that can remove the majority of heads without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Specialized attention heads are most important for translation and can be identified, while many heads are redundant and can be pruned without serious performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small subset of attention heads are important for translation.
Important heads have specialized and interpretable functions, such as attending to adjacent tokens, specific syntactic relations, and rare words.
The proposed pruning method can remove the vast majority of heads (e.g., 38 out of 48 encoder heads) with only a small drop in BLEU (0.15).
Encoder self-attention heads are pruned first, while decoder-encoder attention heads are the most important.
Lower decoder layers retain self-attention heads for language modeling, while higher decoder layers retain decoder-encoder attention heads for conditioning on the source sentence.
papers.limitation: The impact of target language morphology on the accuracy of syntactic attention heads is not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate how the pruning method compares to alternative methods of model compression in neural machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Multi-head self-attention is a key component of the Transformer, a
state-of-the-art architecture for neural machine translation. In this work we
evaluate the contribution made by individual attention heads in the encoder to
the overall performance of the model and analyze the roles played by them. We
find that the most important and confident heads play consistent and often
linguistically-interpretable roles. When pruning heads using a method based on
stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty, we observe
that specialized heads are last to be pruned. Our novel pruning method removes
the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance. For
example, on the English-Russian WMT dataset, pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads
results in a drop of only 0.15 BLEU.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: On the Multilingual Ability of Decoder-based Pre-trained Language Models: Finding and Controlling Language-Specific Neurons
papers.research_question: How do decoder-based pre-trained language models handle multilingualism? Specifically, do language-specific neurons exist and how can they be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the existence of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs and shows that intervening on these neurons can control the language of generated text.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the activity of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs, showing their existence and controllability, which can facilitate deeper understanding and future research.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons are unique to each language with little overlap (<5%).
These neurons are mainly distributed in the first and last few layers of the model.
Intervening on a small set of language-specific neurons (top and bottom 1000) can drastically change the probability of generating text in the target language.
The distribution pattern of language-specific neurons is consistent across languages and model variants.
For conditional text generation (machine translation), intervention on language-specific neurons can improve translation accuracy and BLEU score for some models (like Llama2).
papers.limitation:
Only analyzes open models with publicly available parameters, not closed models like ChatGPT or GPT-4.
Focuses on only six languages; other languages need to be examined in future studies.
Does not analyze encoder-decoder-based PLMs (e.g., mT5) due to architectural differences.
future_direction: Proposing language-specific model-compression methods.
Proposing new fine-tuning methods for downstream tasks to facilitate generalization to languages not included in the training dataset (e.g., only fine-tuning the middle-layer parameters).
Analysis of encoder-decoder-based PLMs remains important for future work.
papers.abstract: Current decoder-based pre-trained language models (PLMs) successfully demonstrate multilingual capabilities. However, it is unclear how these models handle multilingualism. We analyze the neuron-level internal behavior of multilingual decoder-based PLMs, Specifically examining the existence of neurons that fire ``uniquely for each language'' within decoder-only multilingual PLMs. We analyze six languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese, and show that language-specific neurons are unique, with a slight overlap (< 5%) between languages. These neurons are mainly distributed in the models' first and last few layers. This trend remains consistent across languages and models. Additionally, we tamper with less than 1% of the total neurons in each model during inference and demonstrate that tampering with a few language-specific neurons drastically changes the probability of target language occurrence in text generation.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers. Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Disentangling Language and Culture for Evaluating Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to evaluate multilingual large language models by disentangling linguistic medium and cultural context, and explores the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon where models perform better when questions are culturally aligned with the language.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Dual Evaluation Framework that disentangles language and culture to evaluate multilingual LLMs, and discovers the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon where models perform better when questions are culturally aligned with the language.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon, challenging the assumption that LLMs perform uniformly across languages, and highlight the necessity of culturally and linguistically aware model evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
Models perform best on English-speaking culture questions, even when asked in other languages.
Models exhibit Cultural-Linguistic Synergy: better performance when questions are posed in the language corresponding to the cultural context.
A higher proportion of language-specialized neurons are activated when the cultural context aligns with the language, explaining the synergy.
The proportion of specialized neurons can be used as an indicator for comparing multilingual capabilities during training.
The number of activated neurons is strongly correlated with model performance in the corresponding language.
papers.limitation:
The framework requires dual-format question content for robust cross-cultural comparisons, which may not always be available.
The study focuses on a single cultural context per language, not capturing the diversity within languages spoken in multiple regions.
Interpretability probing is limited to smaller models (e.g., 7B and 8B parameters) due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Expand the framework to incorporate more varied cultural contexts for each language.
Extend interpretability analysis to larger models with more parameters.
Further expand the framework for more comprehensive evaluations of multilingual models.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a Dual Evaluation Framework to comprehensively assess the multilingual capabilities of LLMs. By decomposing the evaluation along the dimensions of linguistic medium and cultural context, this framework enables a nuanced analysis of LLMs' ability to process questions within both native and cross-cultural contexts cross-lingually. Extensive evaluations are conducted on a wide range of models, revealing a notable "CulturalLinguistic Synergy" phenomenon, where models exhibit better performance when questions are culturally aligned with the language. This phenomenon is further explored through interpretability probing, which shows that a higher proportion of specific neurons are activated in a language's cultural context. This activation proportion could serve as a potential indicator for evaluating multilingual performance during model training. Our findings challenge the prevailing notion that LLMs, primarily trained on English data, perform uniformly across languages and highlight the necessity of culturally and linguistically model evaluations. Our code can be found at https://yingjiahao14. github.io/Dual-Evaluation/.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Enhancing Multilingual Text Understanding viaTransformer-Based Meta-Learning
papers.research_question: How can multilingual text understanding be enhanced by integrating structured linguistic knowledge (syntactic and semantic) into transformer-based models via meta-learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel framework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning via a Grammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, enhancing multilingual text understanding by aligning neural attention mechanisms with syntactic dependencies.
papers.conclusion: The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA into a transformer-based meta-learning framework significantly improves multilingual text understanding, though limitations exist in handling noisy language and reliance on syntactic annotations.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model (LexiStruct with GIRA) outperforms baseline methods on multiple multilingual benchmarks (XNLI, MLDoc, TyDiQAt, WikiAnn) across metrics like NDCG, Recall, MRR, and Hit Rate.
Ablation studies show that key components (Syntactic Structure Injection, Syntax-Semantics Alignment, Grammar-Semantics Alignment) are essential for the model's performance, with removal of any leading to significant drops in metrics.
The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA improves the model's robustness and interpretability in multilingual understanding tasks.
papers.limitation:
The integration of grammatical constraints may reduce the model's flexibility in handling less-structured or noisy language inputs, such as colloquialisms or code-switching phenomena.
The current implementation assumes access to high-quality syntactic annotations, which may not be available for all languages, especially low-resource ones.
future_direction: Explore strategies for relaxing the assumption of high-quality syntactic annotations, possibly through unsupervised or semi-supervised learning of syntactic structures.
Extend the model's adaptability to more diverse and informal language domains to improve broader applicability in real-world multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the evolving landscape of computational sciences, the integration of structured linguistic knowledge into deep learningmodels has become increasingly vital for advancing multilingual text understanding. Traditional transformer-based architectures,while powerful, often lack the capacity to inherently capture the syntactic and semantic nuances present across diverselanguages, leading to limitations in generalization and interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce a novelframework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning. Our approach employsa structure-aware neural language model that incorporates grammatical constraints directly into the learning process,enhancing the model’s ability to comprehend and process multilingual data effectively. Central to our methodology is theGrammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, which aligns neural attention mechanisms with syntacticdependencies, ensuring that the model’s internal representations adhere to linguistic structures. Experimental evaluationsdemonstrate that our model achieves superior performance in multilingual understanding tasks, exhibiting enhanced robustnessinterpretability. This work contributes to the field by offering a principled method that bridges the gap between statistical learningand linguistic theory, aligning with the journal’s commitment to advancing both fundamental and applied computational sciences.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Interrogating the Explanatory Power of Attention in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: To what extent is attention a reliable source of information for explaining the decisions made by a neural machine translation model?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not a reliable explanation for model decisions in neural machine translation, as many output tokens can be generated even with counterfactual attention weights that suggest contradictory explanations.
papers.conclusion: Using attention weights to justify a model's prediction is not a reliable approach because alternative, contradictory attention weights can yield the same output.
papers.key_findings:
68% of function words and 21% of content words can be generated with counterfactual attention weights, indicating attention is unreliable for explanation.
Generation of function words relies more on target context, while content words rely more on source context.
EOS token generation cannot be reliably explained by attention weights; it depends on special hidden units tracking translation length.
The last encoder state is a poor representation of the source context in an attentional model.
86% of tokens can be generated by only using the source hidden state with maximum attention and using other states uniformly, suggesting highly tuned attention weights may not be necessary.
future_direction: Study the extent to which attention weights correlate with importance measured by gradient-based methods.
Extend findings to other categories such as parts of speech (POS) or out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words.
Address interpretability of copy mechanism in NMT.
Prove the correlation between attention and model predictions in more sophisticated attention models such as Transformer.
papers.abstract: Attention models have become a crucial component in neural machine translation (NMT). They are often implicitly or explicitly used to justify the model's decision in generating a specific token but it has not yet been rigorously established to what extent attention is a reliable source of information in NMT. To evaluate the explanatory power of attention for NMT, we examine the possibility of yielding the same prediction but with counterfactual attention models that modify crucial aspects of the trained attention model. Using these counterfactual attention mechanisms we assess the extent to which they still preserve the generation of function and content words in the translation process. Compared to a state of the art attention model, our counterfactual attention models produce 68% of function words and 21% of content words in our German-English dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that attention models by themselves cannot reliably explain the decisions made by a NMT model. 1

papers.title: Languages Transferred Within the Encoder: On Representation Transfer in Zero-Shot Multilingual Translation
papers.research_question: How does representation transfer occur in multilingual neural machine translation models, and why does zero-shot translation deficiency arise?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in multilingual NMT, the encoder transfers representations to the target language subspace rather than a language-agnostic state, and zero-shot deficiency arises from entanglements. It proposes LOLE and LCLR methods to improve representation transfer and zero-shot translation performance.
papers.conclusion: The encoder transfers representations to the target language subspace, and the proposed LOLE and LCLR methods improve zero-shot translation by enhancing representation transfer.
papers.key_findings:
The encoder transfers translation representations into the target language subspace, not to a language-agnostic state.
Zero-shot translation deficiency occurs because representations become entangled across languages in the encoder, hindering effective transfer to the target language.
Identity pairs serve as a valid base measure for analyzing language representations in MNMT models.
The proposed LOLE method biases encoder representations towards target language subspaces, improving transfer.
The proposed LCLR method enhances the decoder's capacity to distinguish languages, further improving zero-shot translation.
papers.limitation:
The identity pair analysis is based on bi-directional training; unidirectional training may yield different results.
The analysis is conducted on Transformer architecture; other architectures may exhibit different behaviors.
papers.abstract: Understanding representation transfer in multilingual neural machine translation (MNMT) can reveal the reason for the zero-shot translation deficiency. In this work, we systematically analyze the representational issue of MNMT models. We first introduce the identity pair, translating a sentence to itself, to address the lack of the base measure in multilingual investigations, as the identity pair can reflect the representation of a language within the model. Then, we demonstrate that the encoder transfers the source language to the representational subspace of the target language instead of the language-agnostic state. Thus, the zero-shot translation deficiency arises because the representation of a translation is entangled with other languages and not transferred to the target language effectively. Based on our findings, we propose two methods: 1) low-rank language-specific embedding at the encoder, and 2) language-specific contrastive learning of the representation at the decoder. The experimental results on Europarl-15, TED-19, and OPUS-100 datasets show that our methods substantially enhance the performance of zero-shot translations without sacrifices in supervised directions by improving language transfer capacity, thereby providing practical evidence to support our conclusions. Codes are available at https://github.com/zhiqu22/ZeroTrans.

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: CRANE: Causal Relevance Analysis of Language-Specific Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are language capabilities organized at the neuron level in multilingual LLMs? The paper redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity and proposes a method to identify language-specific neurons.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CRANE, a relevance-based framework for identifying language-specific neurons by functional necessity, and finds asymmetric, language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations in multilingual LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CRANE provides a framework for studying language-specific neurons based on functional necessity, revealing that language-specific neurons are language-selective but non-exclusive, and highlighting the importance of distinguishing statistical correlation from functional contribution.
papers.key_findings:
CRANE induces targeted functional degradation on the intended language while preserving performance on non-target languages, outperforming activation-based methods like LAPE.
