Neuron-level interventions reveal an asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations.
Normalized kurtosis of relevance distributions reveals language-related structure in neuron contributions.
Neuron sets identified on the Base model retain functional influence when transferred to the Chat model, indicating partial preservation of language-specific neurons after instruction tuning.
The proposed LangSpec-F1 metric quantifies language-selective functional effects under neuron intervention.
papers.limitation:
CRANE currently relies on normalized kurtosis to characterize concentration patterns in language-conditioned relevance distributions, which is only one possible statistic.
Functional validation is performed via neuron masking, a relatively coarse intervention; more fine-grained causal techniques may provide deeper insight.
Experiments focus on three languages and a single model family, and open-ended generation evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge protocol which may introduce variance.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to broader language coverage, additional architectures, and alternative evaluation paradigms.
Using more fine-grained causal techniques, such as neuron re-weighting or path-specific analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across languages, yet how language capabilities are organized at the neuron level remains poorly understood. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. We propose CRANE, a relevance-based analysis framework that redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity, identifying language-specific neurons through targeted neuron-level interventions. CRANE characterizes neuron specialization by their contribution to language-conditioned predictions rather than activation magnitude. Our implementation will be made publicly available. Neuron-level interventions reveal a consistent asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages to a substantial extent, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations. Experiments on English, Chinese, and Vietnamese across multiple benchmarks, together with a dedicated relevance-based metric and base-to-chat model transfer analysis, show that CRANE isolates language-specific components more precisely than activation-based methods.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Towards a Deep Understanding of Multilingual End-to-End Speech Translation
papers.research_question: Does multilingual end-to-end speech translation exhibit properties similar to multilingual neural machine translation? How are learned representations distributed across languages and layers? Can the model predict linguistic typology features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes multilingual end-to-end speech translation using SVCCA, finding that data quantity is more crucial than linguistic similarity for low-resource languages, and that encoder representations are effective for predicting phonetic typology features.
papers.conclusion: The amount of available data plays a significant role in limiting knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual speech translation. The model's encoder representations perform better on phonetic-related typology features compared to syntax features.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity loses its efficacy in multilingual speech translation when the training data for a specific language is limited.
Enhanced encoder representations and well-aligned audio-text data significantly improve translation quality, surpassing bilingual counterparts when training data is sufficient.
The encoder representations of multilingual speech translation demonstrate superior performance in predicting phonetic features in linguistic typology prediction.
Low-resource languages do not benefit from high-resource languages due to the lack of sufficient data to form language-specific sub-spaces.
Languages from the same language branch tend to cluster together in the representation space as layers deepen.
papers.limitation:
The quality of the LASER-based evaluation datasets may be compromised due to a lower threshold for semantic equivalence, potentially affecting SVCCA analysis reliability.
The analysis lacks a phonological perspective due to the absence of a reliable standard mapping between audio and phoneme, especially for low-resource languages.
future_direction: Addressing data scarcity in the multilingual setting to improve translation quality.
Improving the representation space for individual languages, especially for low-resource languages.
Learning high-quality representation spaces for low-resource languages with limited data to achieve linguistic fairness.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we employ Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA) to analyze representations learnt in a multilingual end-to-end speech translation model trained over 22 languages. SVCCA enables us to estimate representational similarity across languages and layers, enhancing our understanding of the functionality of multilingual speech translation and its potential connection to multilingual neural machine translation. The multilingual speech translation model is trained on the CoVoST 2 dataset in all possible directions, and we utilize LASER to extract parallel bitext data for SVCCA analysis. We derive three major findings from our analysis: (I) Linguistic similarity loses its efficacy in multilingual speech translation when the training data for a specific language is limited. (II) Enhanced encoder representations and well-aligned audio-text data significantly improve translation quality, surpassing the bilingual counterparts when the training data is not compromised. (III) The encoder representations of multilingual speech translation demonstrate superior performance in predicting phonetic features in linguistic typology prediction. With these findings, we propose that releasing the constraint of limited data for low-resource languages and subsequently combining them with linguistically related high-resource languages could offer a more effective approach for multilingual end-to-end speech translation.

papers.title: Different types of syntactic agreement recruit the same units within large language models
papers.research_question: We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that syntactic agreement phenomena recruit overlapping units in large language models, suggesting that agreement forms a functional category, and this pattern holds across languages with overlap correlating with syntactic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that syntactic agreement constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces, with shared units across agreement types and languages, organized by syntactic similarity.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax-responsive units are consistently identified across sentence instances for each syntactic phenomenon and causally support model performance.
Different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units in English.
The overlap among agreement units is higher than with non-agreement phenomena, indicating agreement as a shared functional category.
This pattern replicates in Russian and Chinese, with agreement units showing cross-lingual overlap.
Cross-lingual unit overlap for subject-verb agreement increases with syntactic similarity across 57 languages.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on top-n% unit localization may overlook more distributed syntactic representations.
Analyses are primarily correlational, though causal involvement is demonstrated via ablation.
Focus on benchmarks comparing grammatical to ungrammatical sentences, which may not capture full grammatical knowledge.
future_direction: Apply the approach to other syntactic phenomena, including infrequent structures, ambiguities, and long-distance dependencies.
Extend experiments to other languages with BLiMP-like benchmarks, such as Dutch or Turkish.
Investigate the relationship between syntax and semantics in model representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reliably distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, but how grammatical knowledge is represented within the models remains an open question. We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs. Using a functional localization approach inspired by cognitive neuroscience, we identify the LLM units most responsive to 67 English syntactic phenomena in seven open-weight models. These units are consistently recruited across sentences containing the phenomena and causally support the models' syntactic performance. Critically, different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units, suggesting that agreement constitutes a meaningful functional category for LLMs. This pattern holds in English, Russian, and Chinese; and further, in a cross-lingual analysis of 57 diverse languages, structurally more similar languages share more units for subject-verb agreement. Taken together, these findings reveal that syntactic agreement-a critical marker of syntactic dependencies-constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: Counterfactually Probing Language Identity in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is language identity encoded and used in multilingual language models, and can it be causally manipulated to affect the language of generated tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Language identity is linearly encoded in multilingual models and can be causally manipulated via counterfactual probing to systematically increase the probability of words from a target language in masked language modeling, but not specifically towards translation-equivalent words.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R have both language-specific and language-general components, and counterfactual probing (AlterRep) can be fruitfully applied to manipulate language identity in these models.
papers.key_findings:
Pushing token embeddings towards a target language (e.g., Spanish) in a template of another language (e.g., English) increases the probability of words from the target language and decreases the probability of words from the template language.
Pushing embeddings in the same direction as the template language does not significantly increase the probability of the target word but makes the model more likely to generate words from that language overall.
The manipulation leaves words from a third control language largely unaffected, indicating specificity.
The results hold for both monolingual and code-mixed training data, and for language pairs with different scripts and families.
The findings provide evidence that multilingual models contain both language-specific and language-general components.
papers.limitation:
Techniques like INLP extract only linearly extractable information; more complex non-linear methods might be needed for other properties.
The method is sensitive to parameters like α and the number of INLP iterations, and choosing them is non-trivial.
The results do not demonstrate practical utility for tasks like machine translation.
future_direction: Exploring the use of more complex, non-linear methods (like those proposed by Ravfogel et al., 2022) for manipulating model representations.
Applying the method to explore linguistic typology in multilingual model space.
Translating the results into practical applications.
papers.abstract: Techniques in causal analysis of language models illuminate how linguistic information is organized in LLMs.We use one such technique, AlterRep, a method of counterfactual probing, to explore the internal structure of multilingual models (mBERT and XLM-R).We train a linear classifier on a binary language identity task, to classify tokens between Language X and Language Y. Applying a counterfactual probing procedure, we use the classifier weights to project the embeddings into the null space and push the resulting embeddings either in the direction of Language X or Language Y. Then we evaluate on a masked language modeling task.We find that, given a template in Language X, pushing towards Language Y systematically increases the probability of Language Y words, above and beyond a third-party control language.But it does not specifically push the model towards translation-equivalent words in Language Y. Pushing towards Language X (the same direction as the template) has a minimal effect, but somewhat degrades these models.Overall, we take these results as further evidence of the rich structure of massive multilingual language models, which include both a language-specific and language-general component.And we show that counterfactual probing can be fruitfully applied to multilingual models.

papers.title: Beyond English-Centric LLMs: What Language Do Multilingual Language Models Think in?
papers.research_question: What internal latent language do non-English-centric large language models use in their intermediate layers when processing tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This study demonstrates that the internal latent language of LLMs is determined by their training corpora, with Japanese-specific models using Japanese as a latent language. For non-dominant target languages, models activate the latent language most closely related to it, and the transition from latent to target language occurs in sparse dimensions related to language identity.
papers.conclusion: The internal latent language of LLMs is majorly determined by the language of its training corpora. The transition from latent to target language involves sparse dimensions related to language identity, providing insights for understanding model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Japanese-specific models (Swallow, LLM-jp) use Japanese as an internal latent language when processing Japanese, unlike English-centric Llama-2.
When processing non-dominant languages (French, Chinese), Swallow and LLM-jp exhibit dual internal latent languages (English and Japanese), preferring the one more closely related to the target language.
In culture-conflict QA tasks, intermediate layers initially produce answers biased by the culture of the internal latent language before aligning with the target language context.
The shift from internal latent language to target language representation occurs only in sparse dimensions of the hidden vectors, which are inferred to be related to language identity.
papers.limitation: An exception in Swallow's translation results (higher Japanese probability for French target than Chinese) may be due to specific content in its training corpus, but this hypothesis is difficult to verify.
future_direction: Extend investigation to models with other specific dominant languages, such as Chinese, French, and Arabic.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether non-English-centric LLMs, despite their strong performance, `think' in their respective dominant language: more precisely, `think' refers to how the representations of intermediate layers, when un-embedded into the vocabulary space, exhibit higher probabilities for certain dominant languages during generation. We term such languages as internal $\textbf{latent languages}$. We examine the latent language of three typical categories of models for Japanese processing: Llama2, an English-centric model; Swallow, an English-centric model with continued pre-training in Japanese; and LLM-jp, a model pre-trained on balanced English and Japanese corpora. Our empirical findings reveal that, unlike Llama2 which relies exclusively on English as the internal latent language, Japanese-specific Swallow and LLM-jp employ both Japanese and English, exhibiting dual internal latent languages. For any given target language, the model preferentially activates the latent language most closely related to it. In addition, we explore how intermediate layers respond to questions involving cultural conflicts between latent internal and target output languages. We further explore how the language identity shifts across layers while keeping consistent semantic meaning reflected in the intermediate layer representations. This study deepens the understanding of non-English-centric large language models, highlighting the intricate dynamics of language representation within their intermediate layers.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language\n Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in neural language models, specifically how do models prefer grammatical inflections and do neurons process agreement similarly across different syntactic structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that language models use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement depending on whether the subject and verb are adjacent, and that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences.
papers.conclusion: The study applies causal mediation analysis to reveal mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in pre-trained language models, showing how neurons are implicated and providing insights into model inner workings.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 and Transformer-XL use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement: one for adjacent subject-verb pairs and another for non-adjacent pairs, while XLNet uses a unified mechanism.
Larger models have more distributed agreement mechanisms across layers, but do not always have stronger preferences for correct inflections.
The overlap of high-NIE neurons across syntactic structures correlates with human intuitions of syntactic similarity.
Plural subjects consistently have higher grammaticality values than singular subjects across structures.
Adverbial distractors increase the probability of correct verb inflections more than incorrect ones, while attractors decrease total effects.
future_direction: Intervening on groups of neurons and attention heads to see how components work together
Extending the analysis to phenomena such as filler-gap dependencies and negative polarity items
Examining the impact of specific verbs on syntactic agreement mechanisms
papers.abstract:
Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language
models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate
the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies
causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate
the magnitude of models' preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as
whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with
different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across
architectures and model sizes -- notably, that larger models do not necessarily
learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for
producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the
input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of
neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Encoders Learn Cross-lingual Representation?
papers.research_question: How do multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations without explicit cross-lingual signals, and what factors influence this process?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation provides a comprehensive analysis of how multilingual encoders like mBERT learn cross-lingual representations, identifying key factors such as parameter sharing, anchor points, and language similarity, and proposes methods like contrastive alignment to improve cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations through shared parameters and anchor points, but performance is uneven across languages, and explicit alignment can help. Future work includes scaling to more languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual BERT (mBERT) learns cross-lingual representations without any explicit cross-lingual signal, achieving strong zero-shot transfer across a variety of tasks.
Parameter sharing and anchor points (shared subwords across languages) are crucial for the emergence of cross-lingual representations in multilingual encoders.
Not all languages are equally represented in mBERT; low-resource languages suffer from poor performance due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
Explicit alignment methods, such as contrastive alignment using bitext, can improve cross-lingual representations, but their effectiveness varies across models and language pairs.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exhibits high variance due to underspecified optimization, and data projection with self-training can constrain and improve transfer performance.
papers.limitation: mBERT performs poorly on low-resource languages due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Continue scaling multilingual encoders to more languages and larger models
Extend to multimodal multilingual models
Improve cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages
papers.abstract: NLP systems typically require support for more than one language. As different languages have different amounts of supervision, cross-lingual transfer benefits languages with little to no training data by transferring from other languages. From an engineering perspective, multilingual NLP benefits development and maintenance by serving multiple languages with a single system. Both cross-lingual transfer and multilingual NLP rely on cross-lingual representations serving as the foundation. As BERT revolutionized representation learning and NLP, it also revolutionized cross-lingual representations and cross-lingual transfer. Multilingual BERT was released as a replacement for single-language BERT, trained with Wikipedia data in 104 languages. Surprisingly, without any explicit cross-lingual signal, multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual representations in addition to representations for individual languages. This thesis first shows such surprising cross-lingual effectiveness compared against prior art on various tasks. Naturally, it raises a set of questions, most notably how do these multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations. In exploring these questions, this thesis will analyze the behavior of multilingual models in a variety of settings on high and low resource languages. We also look at how to inject different cross-lingual signals into multilingual encoders, and the optimization behavior of cross-lingual transfer with these models. Together, they provide a better understanding of multilingual encoders on cross-lingual transfer. Our findings will lead us to suggested improvements to multilingual encoders and cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs have specialized language heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs have specialized language attention heads, and can language-specific heads be removed without degrading performance in targeted languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs have language-specific and language-agnostic attention heads, and suggests that pruning language-specific heads for unwanted languages may be possible without harming performance in desired languages.
papers.conclusion: The study evaluates attention head behavior in a multilingual LLM and identifies distinct types of heads, supporting the potential for efficient deployment through selective pruning.
papers.key_findings:
There are four types of attention heads: English-specific, Hindi-specific, language-agnostic, and miscellaneous.
Masking certain attention heads can decrease model accuracy on specific questions.
Masking other attention heads can increase model accuracy by correcting mistakes.
Language-specific heads contribute only to their respective languages, while language-agnostic heads contribute to both.
Some heads have no effect on the evaluated languages, possibly due to being specific to other languages or activating on unseen patterns.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to the last few layers and only 500 examples per language, which may not fully capture head contributions.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) have gained significant popularity for their ability to process and generate text across multiple languages. However, deploying these models in production can be inefficient when only a subset of the supported languages is of interest. There has been some research conducted on identifying whether machine translation models have language-specific or language-agnostic heads, however no research has been conducted for multilingual LLMs, to the best of our knowledge, that as we know are capable of performing diverse tasks beyond just translation. This paper explores whether multilingual LLMs have specialized language attention heads for each language, and investigates the possibility of removing language-specific heads for unwanted languages without degrading performance in the targeted languages. Our findings could inform more efficient deployment strategies for multilingual LLMs, enabling reduced model complexity while maintaining high accuracy for targeted languages.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Similarity of Sentence Representations in Multilingual LMs: Resolving Conflicting Literature and a Case Study of Baltic Languages
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models internally represent different languages, and do they converge to a shared cross-lingual space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper resolves conflicting literature by showing that multilingual LMs project languages into a shared cross-lingual space when using mean-pooling and CKA/SVCCA, and finds that Baltic languages are part of this space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mean-pooling with SVCCA/CKA is optimal for cross-lingual representational similarity analysis, and while most languages share a cross-lingual space, Baltic languages are part of it.
papers.key_findings:
CLS-pooling with PWCCA gives divergent patterns, while mean-pooling with CKA/SVCCA shows convergence in cross-lingual similarity.
Mean-pooling is more effective than CLS-pooling for cross-lingual representational analysis, as shown by probing tasks.
Not all languages share the cross-lingual space equally; some like Urdu and Hindi are outliers.
Baltic languages (Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian) are grouped and belong to the shared cross-lingual space.
The most cross-lingual layer for XLM-R is the 7th layer.
future_direction: Finding the exact criteria for exclusion of languages from the shared cross-lingual space.
papers.abstract: Low-resource languages, such as Baltic languages, benefit from Large Multilingual Models (LMs) that possess remarkable cross-lingual transfer performance capabilities. This work is an interpretation and analysis study into cross-lingual representations of Multilingual LMs. Previous works hypothesized that these LMs internally project representations of different languages into a shared cross-lingual space. However, the literature produced contradictory results. In this paper, we revisit the prior work claiming that "BERT is not an Interlingua" and show that different languages do converge to a shared space in such language models with another choice of pooling strategy or similarity index. Then, we perform cross-lingual representational analysis for the two most popular multilingual LMs employing 378 pairwise language comparisons. We discover that while most languages share joint cross-lingual space, some do not. However, we observe that Baltic languages do belong to that shared space.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like the Brain? Sentence-Level Evidences from Layer-Wise Embeddings and fMRI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity is due to model scaling or deeper alignment with human language processing principles.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that instruction tuning and semantic comprehension ability, rather than model scale alone, drive the alignment between LLM representations and human brain activity during sentence processing.
papers.conclusion: Instruction tuning and semantic comprehension capacity, not merely parameter size, are key drivers of neural similarity, and the alignment is anatomically and functionally specific to intermediate layers and hemispheric specializations.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of LLMs show higher correlation with brain activity than final layers.
Instruction-tuned models exhibit better performance and stronger neural alignment compared to their base versions.
Hemispheric asymmetry in brain regions aligns with functional specialization, with left-hemisphere regions correlating more with core language processing and right-hemisphere regions with higher cognitive functions.
future_direction: Training procedures that explicitly target alignment with brain data to produce more cognitively plausible models.
Developing hybrid neuro-symbolic LLMs to better reflect distributed and lateralized processing patterns observed in the brain.
papers.abstract: Understanding whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain converge on similar computational principles remains a fundamental and important question in cognitive neuroscience and AI. Do the brain-like patterns observed in LLMs emerge simply from scaling, or do they reflect deeper alignment with the architecture of human language processing? This study focuses on the sentence-level neural mechanisms of language models, systematically investigating how layer-wise representations in LLMs align with the dynamic neural responses during human sentence comprehension. By comparing hierarchical embeddings from 14 publicly available LLMs with fMRI data collected from participants, who were exposed to a naturalistic narrative story, we constructed sentence-level neural prediction models to identify the model layers most significantly correlated with brain region activations. Results show that improvements in model performance drive the evolution of representational architectures toward brain-like hierarchies, particularly achieving stronger functional and anatomical correspondence at higher semantic abstraction levels. These findings advance our understanding of the computational parallels between LLMs and the human brain, highlighting the potential of LLMs as models for human language processing.

papers.title: Improving In-context Learning of Multilingual Generative Language Models with Cross-lingual Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we improve cross-lingual in-context learning and mitigate performance bias between languages in multilingual generative models using limited parallel data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a cross-lingual alignment framework (AFP) that uses multilingual contrastive learning and cross-lingual instruction following to improve cross-lingual abilities and reduce performance gaps in multilingual generative models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AFP framework improves cross-lingual capabilities and internal representations of multilingual generative models, reducing performance gaps between languages.
papers.key_findings:
AFP significantly improves cross-lingual in-context learning performance on various tasks with less than 0.1‰ of pre-training tokens.
AFP mitigates the internal representation gap between languages, leading to better-aligned and more uniform multilingual representations.
Cross-lingual instruction following (CIF) is more effective than multilingual instruction tuning (MIT) for cross-lingual ability.
AFP also improves performance on unseen languages for models like Llama that are pre-trained mainly on English.
The framework is effective across different model scales and architectures.
papers.limitation:
Relies on labeled parallel data, which is unavailable for languages without parallel samples.
Limited to models with up to 7.5B parameters due to computational constraints.
Error propagation from the machine translation system used may result in inferior performance.
future_direction: Extend the framework to align different modalities in multi-modal generative models.
Develop unsupervised multilingual alignment methods.
papers.abstract: Multilingual generative models obtain remarkable cross-lingual in-context learning capabilities through pre-training on large-scale corpora. However, they still exhibit a performance bias toward high-resource languages and learn isolated distributions of multilingual sentence representations, which may hinder knowledge transfer across languages. To bridge this gap, we propose a simple yet effective cross-lingual alignment framework exploiting pairs of translation sentences. It aligns the internal sentence representations across different languages via multilingual contrastive learning and aligns outputs by following cross-lingual instructions in the target language. Experimental results show that even with less than 0.1 {\textperthousand} of pre-training tokens, our alignment framework significantly boosts the cross-lingual abilities of generative language models and mitigates the performance gap. Further analyses reveal that it results in a better internal multilingual representation distribution of multilingual models.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Multilingual Knowledge Editing with Language-Agnostic Factual Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously edit factual knowledge across multiple languages in large language models while avoiding knowledge conflicts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LU-LAFNs, a method for multilingual knowledge editing by identifying and updating language-agnostic factual neurons in LLMs, which avoids knowledge conflicts and improves edit performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies language-agnostic factual neurons in LLMs and proposes the LU-LAFNs method for effective multilingual knowledge editing, which avoids conflicts and achieves superior performance on benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-agnostic factual neurons (LAFNs) exist in LLMs and represent factual knowledge shared across languages.
LU-LAFNs achieves the best edit performance on Bi-ZsRE and MzsRE benchmarks compared to existing methods.
The method avoids knowledge conflicts by modeling semantic connections between multilingual knowledge through shared neurons.
Edit performance is influenced by LLMs' inherent language capabilities and the selection of layers for updating.
Using paraphrases during the locating stage improves edit performance by precisely identifying relevant neurons.
papers.limitation:
Requires aligned multilingual knowledge and subjects, which may need preprocessing if not available in datasets.
Exact-match for cache subject matching is too strict and will be optimized to fuzzy matching in future work.
Poor performance on the Portability metric, indicating limited reasoning ability based on edited knowledge.
future_direction: Optimize cache subject matching to a fuzzy matching method.
Improve the method for reasoning scenarios, such as testing on the CROLIN-MQUAKE benchmark.
papers.abstract: Multilingual knowledge editing (MKE) aims to simultaneously update factual knowledge across multiple languages within large language models (LLMs). Previous research indicates that the same knowledge across different languages within LLMs exhibits a degree of shareability. However, most existing MKE methods overlook the connections of the same knowledge between different languages, resulting in knowledge conflicts and limited edit performance. To address this issue, we first investigate how LLMs process multilingual factual knowledge and discover that the same factual knowledge in different languages generally activates a shared set of neurons, which we call language-agnostic factual neurons (LAFNs). These neurons represent the same factual knowledge shared across languages and imply the semantic connections among multilingual knowledge. Inspired by this finding, we propose a new MKE method by Locating and Updating Language-Agnostic Factual Neurons (LU-LAFNs) to edit multilingual knowledge simultaneously, which avoids knowledge conflicts and thus improves edit performance. Experimental results on Bi-ZsRE and MzsRE benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves the best edit performance, indicating the effectiveness and importance of modeling the semantic connections among multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: SLAM: Towards Efficient Multilingual Reasoning via Selective Language Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently align multilingual reasoning abilities in large language models while avoiding catastrophic forgetting and reducing computational cost?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SLAM, a method that selectively fine-tunes only the lower-level FFN sub-layers responsible for multilingual comprehension, achieving efficient multilingual reasoning alignment in one stage without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: SLAM efficiently achieves multilingual reasoning alignment by selectively fine-tuning lower-level FFN sub-layers, demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency across multiple tasks and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Lower-level layers are responsible for language-specific representations, while higher-level layers create universal representations.
Selectively fine-tuning FFN sub-layers in the first six layers achieves state-of-the-art multilingual reasoning performance with only 6.5-8% of parameters.
SLAM reduces training time by 4.1-11.9x compared to the two-stage full-parameter tuning method.
SLAM generalizes well to out-of-domain mathematical reasoning and to multilingual common sense reasoning.
Increasing the overlap of activated neurons between non-English and English at lower layers improves multilingual comprehension and reasoning alignment.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are primarily conducted on Llama2 series models, limiting generalizability to other model families.
Imbalanced data among languages in the translation dataset leads to performance trade-offs across languages.
future_direction: Extend experiments to additional series models beyond Llama2.
Conduct in-depth analysis of performance trade-offs across languages due to imbalanced data.
papers.abstract: Despite the significant improvements achieved by large language models (LLMs) in English reasoning tasks, these models continue to struggle with multilingual reasoning. Recent studies leverage a full-parameter and two-stage training paradigm to teach models to first understand non-English questions and then reason. However, this method suffers from both substantial computational resource computing and catastrophic forgetting. The fundamental cause is that, with the primary goal of enhancing multilingual comprehension, an excessive number of irrelevant layers and parameters are tuned during the first stage. Given our findings that the representation learning of languages is merely conducted in lower-level layers, we propose an efficient multilingual reasoning alignment approach that precisely identifies and fine-tunes the layers responsible for handling multilingualism. Experimental results show that our method, SLAM, only tunes 6 layers' feed-forward sub-layers including 6.5-8% of all parameters within 7B and 13B LLMs, achieving superior average performance than all strong baselines across 10 languages. Meanwhile, SLAM only involves one training stage, reducing training time by 4.1-11.9 compared to the two-stage method.

papers.title: Recurrent Attention for the Transformer
papers.research_question: Whether and how an explicit dependency on previous attention decisions should be included in the Transformer encoder-decoder attention mechanism to improve translation performance.
papers.core_contribution: Adding recurrent connections to the Transformer's cross-attention mechanism does not significantly improve translation performance and increases training time, indicating that self-attention already provides sufficient context.
papers.conclusion: Recurrent dependencies in Transformer attention are not beneficial for machine translation, as self-attention already incorporates sufficient context information.
papers.key_findings:
None of the proposed recurrent attention variants significantly outperform the baseline Transformer on machine translation tasks.
Training speed is reduced by at least a factor of 5 due to loss of parallelization in the decoder.
Some variants show slight improvements on the development set but not on test sets, suggesting overfitting.
The 'expand key-value list' variant 1 and 2 performed slightly better than baseline on development set, but not consistently.
Re-scaling attention weights did not lead to significant gains.
papers.limitation:
Training is significantly slower due to breaking parallelization in the decoder.
Hyperparameter tuning may lead to overfitting on the development set.
papers.abstract: In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation on one of the centerpieces of modern machine translation systems: the encoderdecoder attention mechanism. Motivated by the concept of first-order alignments, we extend the (cross-)attention mechanism by a recurrent connection, allowing direct access to previous attention/alignment decisions. We propose several ways to include such a recurrency into the attention mechanism. Verifying their performance across different translation tasks we conclude that these extensions and dependencies are not beneficial for the translation performance of the Transformer architecture.

papers.title: Brain-Language Model Alignment: Insights into the Platonic Hypothesis and Intermediate-Layer Advantage
papers.research_question: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? The paper reviews evidence to test the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.core_contribution: This review of 25 fMRI-based studies provides converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.conclusion: Framing alignment through the dual lenses of the PRH and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage provides a theoretical scaffold for designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment tends to be stronger for larger, higher-performing models and those trained on more tasks, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Cross-modal training reliably enhances alignment by pushing models toward modality-independent conceptual representations.
Intermediate layers of language models show the strongest alignment with brain activity, supporting the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
Fine-tuning (including instruction-tuning and brain-tuning) can improve alignment, but the evidence is not uniformly positive.
Multimodal models, especially vision-language models, align better with brain activity than unimodal models.
papers.limitation: The studies analysed differ in metrics, datasets, and alignment protocols. Such heterogeneity implies that effects of scale or layer depth should be treated as qualitative patterns rather than quantitative laws.
future_direction: Designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.abstract: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? Recent years have seen a rise in studies of neural activations and model alignment. In this work, we review 25 fMRI-based studies published between 2023 and 2025 and explicitly confront their findings with two key hypotheses: (i) the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- that as models scale and improve, they converge to a representation of the real world, and (ii) the Intermediate-Layer Advantage -- that intermediate (mid-depth) layers often encode richer, more generalizable features. Our findings provide converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting both hypotheses and motivating further research on brain-model alignment.

papers.title: A Theoretical Understanding of Self-Correction through In-context Alignment
papers.research_question: How does the self-correction capability arise in large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that transformers can perform self-correction via in-context alignment, and proposes the Checking as Context (CaC) method which applies this insight to alleviate social bias and defend against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-correction in LLMs can be understood as a form of in-context alignment, and transformers possess the inherent architectural capability to perform it, which has practical implications for improving model safety and reducing bias.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can implement gradient descent for common alignment objectives (Bradley-Terry, Plackett-Luce) in-context, providing a mechanism for self-correction.
The quality of the reward signal (critic) is crucial for effective self-correction.
Realistic transformer components (softmax attention, multi-head attention, FFN, stacked layers) are necessary for implementing the ranking and refinement operations required for in-context alignment.
The proposed Checking as Context (CaC) method, based on the theoretical insights, can effectively reduce social bias in model outputs.
CaC can significantly reduce the success rate of various jailbreak attacks without external feedback.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis only considers a simplified self-correction pipeline; in practice, prompt design has a large effect on performance.
future_direction: Further research on understanding, exploiting, and enhancing self-correction for building better foundation models.
Investigating the effect of prompt design on self-correction performance.
papers.abstract: Going beyond mimicking limited human experiences, recent studies show initial evidence that, like humans, large language models (LLMs) are capable of improving their abilities purely by self-correction, i.e., correcting previous responses through self-examination, in certain circumstances. Nevertheless, little is known about how such capabilities arise.
